title: Instrumental, vokativ, mapa
theme: S kahvom and Emire finish with and calling, then one map points the little words at jobs you already own.

whyHere.heading: Why you are here
whyHere.body: Today you add with and calling as the last thing-word jobs, then you hang one map for the little words that pick those jobs. S kahvom means with coffee, and Emire is how you call Emir across the café. English hangs with in front and uses a bare name to shout. Bosnian dresses both, then gives you one chart that points each English habit at a job you already learned.

englishLies.heading: Why English lies
englishLies.body: English lies because with coffee and hey Emir keep coffee and Emir almost still. You add with, or you just raise your voice. Bosnian moves the ending again. Kahva becomes kahvom after s, and Emir becomes Emire when you call him. Schools call those jobs instrumental and vokativ. You can keep saying with and calling. The map at the end is not a new pile. It is a street index for the jobs from Chapters 2 through 5.

knownLine.heading: A line you already say
knownLine.body: Book 1 already called Emir by name with Emire, koliko je sati, which means Emir, what time is it? That e on Emire is today’s calling mark on a he-pile person. The new twin is with. Amira can say Dolazim s kahvom, which means I am coming with coffee, when the cup travels with her. Kahvom is still she. It is not kahvu and not kahve.
knownLine.speaker: Ana

pattern.heading: The pattern
pattern.body: She-pile words swap that final a for om in the with job. Kahva becomes kahvom, and kuća becomes kućom. He-pile words usually take om too, so most becomes mostom and Emir becomes Emirom. Leftover words usually take om or em, so pivo becomes pivom and more becomes morem. Put s or sa in front when English says with. The calling job is smaller than the with job. Emir becomes Emire, Ana often becomes Ano, and Amira often becomes Amiro. Learn s kahvom and Emire first. Then read the map so each little word points at the right older job.

howYouGuess.heading: The pests
howYouGuess.body: Three pests will trip you today. The first is S kahvu, which grabs the want-it form after with when the line needs kahvom. The second is calling Emir while leaving him as Emir in a shout across the room, when the calling form is Emire. The third pest is treating the map as seven new endings to memorize today. The map only points you back. U plus into still means the want-it job, nema still means the of job, and s still means the with job. Read the pointer and reuse the outfit you already own.

trick.heading: The bit that tricks you
trick.body: The trap is to invent a fresh ending every time you see a preposition. Prepositions are pickers, and they do not invent a parallel language. S picks with, iz picks from, and u picks into or in, while the next ending tells you which. The other trap is to mix calling with to. Emire is for calling him, and Emiru is for giving to him. If you hand coffee to Emire, you used the shout form in the give line.

nerd.heading: Why it's like this
nerd.body:
Old English is the English of England about a thousand years ago, not a class you missed. Farmers and priests around Winchester had a with outfit on thing-words and a special calling form on names. Later English mostly dropped both on nouns. You kept with as a free word, and you call people with bare names plus tone of voice. You speak that later version.

Bosnian kept both marks. Instrumental is the with and by-means outfit. Vocative is the calling outfit. The map in this chapter is just honesty about prepositions. In older English the ending did more of the pointing. In your English the little word does more of the pointing. Bosnian still lets the ending finish the job the little word started.

items.prompt: Ana is coming with coffee. Which form after s?
You need to call Emir across the room. Which form?
items.explanation: Emire is calling. Emira was seeing him. Emiru was giving to him.

items.prompt: Emir is going with Ana. Which form?
items.explanation: With Ana is Anom. Ani was to Ana. Ano is calling.

items.prompt: Ana goes by car. Which form?
items.explanation: Autom is the with and by-means form on pest auto.

items.prompt: Someone says S kahvu. What went wrong?
options: They needed the of form kahve.

items.prompt: You hand coffee to Emir while calling him Emire. What went wrong?
options: Calling Emire is not the to form Emiru.
items.explanation: Emire is the shout. Emiru is to Emir.

items.prompt: On the map, nema points to which job?
items.explanation: Nema kahve. The map only points.

items.prompt: On the map, u plus motion into points to which job?
items.explanation: Idem u kuću. Into reuses want-it.

items.prompt: Emir is sitting with beer. Which form?
items.explanation: S pivom. Leftover takes om here.

items.prompt: You call Amira across the cafe. Which form?
items.explanation: Amiro is the everyday calling form for Amira, same shelf as Emire and Ano.

questions.question: S kahvom uses which job?
questions.explanation: Kahvom is the with form. S is the picker.

questions.question: Emire, koliko je sati? Why Emire?
questions.explanation: That shout is the calling job, and Book 1 already used it.

questions.question: Idem s Emirom versus Emire. What is the difference?
options: Emirom is with. Emire is calling.
questions.explanation: With and calling are different outfits.

questions.question: What does the preposition map do?
options: Points little words at jobs you already learned
questions.explanation: The map is an index, not a second grammar.

questions.question: Why is Idem autom correct?
options: Auto is leftover and stays auto
The by-means job takes autom on that he-pile pest
questions.explanation: Autom is with and by means. Pest auto still follows he habits.

questions.question: Calling Ana across the café. Which form?
questions.explanation: Ano is the everyday calling form for Ana, same shelf as Emire and Amiro.

next.body: You now have with and calling, and one map that points iz, nema, u, na, o, and s at the jobs from Chapters 2 to 5. Coffee still lives in the she pile. The outfits are the only news. Chapter 6 is matching words like my that have to ride with kahva when the job changes. The notebook moves from endings on the noun to endings on the words that stick to it.
